intro: If your job requires eye protection, 'looks tough' isn't good enough — the eyewear has to meet a testable standard. In the U.S. that standard is ANSI Z87.1, and prescription safety glasses Z87 combine that certified protection with your vision correction. This guide explains exactly what the Z87 and Z87+ markings mean, which brands (including Oakley prescription safety glasses) offer rated frames, and how the Rx lenses are made.

There's a lot of confusion online about safety marks, so we'll keep it honest and specific. Below you'll learn how to read the stamps on a frame and lens, why polycarbonate is the safety lens material, and how to get a genuinely rated pair — not fashion glasses dressed up to look protective.

sections.h2: Prescription safety glasses Z87: what the markings mean
body: ANSI Z87.1 is the American National Standard for occupational and educational personal eye protection, and OSHA references it for workplace eyewear. To be genuine prescription safety glasses Z87, both the frame and the lenses must be marked — a compliant frame carries a 'Z87' (or 'Z87-2' for prescription) stamp, and the lenses carry the maker's mark plus the impact designation.

Z87 vs. Z87+: A plain Z87 mark meets the basic standard; the Z87+ mark means the eyewear passed high-impact testing (a steel ball fired at high velocity, plus a heavier drop test). For most industrial and impact hazards you want Z87+. Prescription safety frames are also marked Z87-2 to show they're the prescription version.

figure.alt: Reading ANSI Z87.1 markings on prescription safety glasses frame and lens
figure.caption: Genuine safety eyewear is marked on both frame and lens: Z87 (basic), Z87+ (high-impact), and Z87-2 on prescription frames.

subs.body: On the frame, look for the manufacturer's mark and 'Z87' — or 'Z87-2' on a prescription safety frame. On each lens, look for the maker's mark and a '+' if it's high-impact. If the markings aren't there, it isn't certified prescription safety glasses Z87, no matter how rugged it looks.

Certified safety lenses are almost always polycarbonate (or Trivex) — the most impact-resistant everyday lens material. It's what lets a lens pass the Z87+ high-impact tests, and it's standard on real prescription safety glasses.
Many workplaces require side protection. Some Z87 frames have built-in side shields or a wraparound design; others accept clip-on side shields. Your hazard assessment determines what you need.

sections.h2: How Rx safety lenses are made — and what they cost
body: Your prescription goes into a rated safety frame two ways. Milder prescriptions are usually direct-glazed — ground into the polycarbonate safety lens. Stronger prescriptions or deeply curved wrap frames use an Rx insert that holds your prescription lenses behind the protective front lens, keeping the optics accurate while the outer lens takes the impact.

On price, ANSI Z87 prescription safety glasses typically run about $120–$350 for a rated frame with prescription polycarbonate lenses, with premium brands like Oakley, photochromic lenses and Rx inserts toward the top. Many employers reimburse safety eyewear — ask us for a documented quote.

subs.body: Direct-glaze keeps the profile slim for milder prescriptions; an Rx insert handles strong prescriptions and high-wrap safety frames. Both keep the frame's Z87 rating as long as the certified lenses and frame are used together — we'll match the method to your Rx.

faq.q: What does Z87 mean on safety glasses?
faq.a: Z87 means the eyewear meets ANSI Z87.1, the U.S. standard for occupational and educational eye protection. Genuine safety glasses carry the mark on both the frame and the lenses; prescription safety frames are marked Z87-2. The plus sign (Z87+) means the eyewear passed high-impact testing.

faq.q: What's the difference between Z87 and Z87+?
faq.a: A plain Z87 mark meets the basic standard. The Z87+ mark means the eyewear passed high-impact testing — a steel ball fired at high velocity plus a heavier drop test. For most industrial and impact hazards, you want Z87+.

faq.q: Does Oakley make prescription safety glasses?
faq.a: Yes. Oakley offers ANSI Z87.1-compliant frames that can be made with your prescription, so you get Oakley's styling and lens technology with certified eye protection. Ask us which Oakley models carry the Z87 rating.

faq.q: Can prescription safety glasses be Z87 rated?
faq.a: Yes. Both the frame and the certified polycarbonate lenses carry the rating, and prescription safety frames are marked Z87-2. Your prescription is either direct-glazed into the safety lens or held in an Rx insert behind the protective front lens.

faq.q: What lens material is used in Z87 safety glasses?
faq.a: Almost always polycarbonate (or Trivex), the most impact-resistant everyday lens material. It's what allows a lens to pass the Z87+ high-impact tests and is standard on genuine prescription safety glasses.

faq.q: How much do Z87 prescription safety glasses cost?
faq.a: Typically about $120–$350 for a rated frame with prescription polycarbonate lenses. Premium brands like Oakley, photochromic lenses and Rx inserts cost more. Many employers reimburse safety eyewear, so ask us for a documented quote.

faq.q: How do I know my safety glasses are really certified?
faq.a: Check the markings. The frame should be stamped Z87 (or Z87-2 for prescription) with the manufacturer's mark, and each lens should carry the maker's mark and a '+' if it's high-impact. If those marks aren't there, the eyewear isn't certified, no matter how rugged it looks.
